W7222540786.abstract: Abstract The adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to scientific domains requires efficient strategies to mitigate high computational costs while preserving performance. We present a systematic survey of efficiency techniques for adapting LLMs to scientific applications. Our review analyzes 120 studies across seven scientific fields, including biomedicine, clinical medicine, biology, mathematics, chemistry, geo-environmental science, and cross-domain scientific research. Across the surveyed literature, we summarize 34 representative models and 30 scientific datasets for efficient scientific LLM research. Examining parameter-efficient fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, architectural optimization, and data-centric approaches, we introduce a dual-axis taxonomy that organizes efficiency techniques by both methodological strategy and scientific domain. We further provide practical guidance for selecting efficiency strategies under resource constraints and highlight open challenges including multimodal integration, catastrophic forgetting, and automated method selection. By synthesizing cross-domain evidence and outlining directions for sustainable model development, this survey supports the adoption of efficient scientific LLMs in resource-constrained research environments and promotes more accessible and responsible deployment across scientific disciplines.

W7222614784.abstract: As cyberattack sophistication has grown, there is a growing need for intelligent, adaptive threat hunting solutions to accurately detect an array of network intrusions while reducing false alarms.Traditional IDS methods might struggle to generalize across data sets, achieve optimal hyperparameter tuning, or provide sufficient interpretability in the context of large-scale cybersecurity datasets.This study presents a Cyber Threat Hunting Framework based on Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO-RAG-MADRL-Net) to enhance the detection of multiple cyber-attacks of CICIDS2017 benchmark datasets.Proposed framework conducts thorough data pre-processing, mutual information based feature selection, and GWO to search for the optimal hyperparameters of the model, and finally, an optimized XGBoost classifier is used for intelligent threat classification.To further interpret the model decisions, explainable artificial intelligence is implemented based on SHAP to build transparency and feature level understanding.The experimental results show high accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC for the proposed framework, which are equal to 99.57%, 99.57%, 99.57%, 99.57%, 99.98%, and 99.93% respectively, demonstrating the highly reliable detection of different cyberattacks.The results of the optimized framework are compared with Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Extra Trees, and LightGBM, showing its effectiveness in providing strong classification performance and better discriminative capability.The proposed solution can be efficiently and scalably implemented at an enterprise level to detect intelligent threats in real-time network security scenarios, and it is interpretable.

W7222620584.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), first-principles computational methods, and advanced functional materials provides new opportunities for the accelerated discovery of energy-efficient quantum and spintronic materials. Heusler alloys are particularly attractive because their chemical composition and structural ordering can be systematically modified to obtain desirable magnetic, electronic, topological, and thermoelectric properties. Magnetic Heusler compounds with strong spin–orbit coupling can exhibit Weyl points, band crossings, Berry-curvature hotspots, and enhanced anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) and anomalous Nernst conductivity (ANC). Representative literature systems demonstrate the potential of this materials family: Co2MnGa has a reported calculated AHC of approximately −1310 Scm⁻¹, while Co2MnAl reaches approximately −1631 Scm⁻¹; Co2CrAl illustrates strong Fermi-level dependence, with its AHC increasing from approximately −313 Scm⁻¹ to about 1089 Scm⁻¹ after energy tuning. This work proposes an integrated density functional theory (DFT) and AI framework for the systematic discovery and optimization of sustainable topological Heusler materials. DFT calculations provide the physics-based evaluation of structural stability, magnetic ordering, electronic structure, spin–orbit coupling, Berry curvature, AHC, and ANC, while machine-learning models can learn composition–structure–property relationships and accelerate screening across unexplored chemical spaces. The proposed workflow includes stability screening, magnetic-ground-state analysis, electronic and topological characterization, Berry-curvature calculations, anomalous transverse transport calculations, machine-learning prediction, and independent DFT validation. Chemical substitution and carrier tuning are considered as strategies for positioning topological features near the Fermi level and enhancing transverse transport. Literature examples such as Pt2CrRh, with reported AHC of approximately 1966 Scm⁻¹ and ANC of approximately 7.50 Am⁻¹K⁻¹, and (Co0. 8Ni0.2)2FeSn, with reported AHC of approximately −2568 Scm⁻¹ and ANC of approximately 8.27 Am⁻¹K⁻¹, illustrate the potential of chemical tuning for achieving large transverse responses. The proposed DFT–AI strategy can therefore provide an efficient route toward identifying promising materials for spintronics, spin-caloritronics, low-power electronics, and thermal-energy conversion.

W7222660053.abstract: Gravitational-wave (GW) astronomy relies on the ability to extract very weak, short and/or long duration signals from nonstationary and non-Gaussian detector noise. While matched filtering is the benchmark technique for modeled compact-binary signals, the number of templates and the complexity of the source model increases the amount of computation required. Machine learning (ML) methods, in particular convolutional neural networks, residual networks, autoencoders, attention mechanisms and hybrid classifiers, have therefore been explored for low latency detection and denoising, glitch rejection, anomaly discovery, and rapid parameter estimation. This paper provides a structured narrative synthesis of 50 DOI-indexed studies and sets up methodological framework of credible searches of GW using ML. While the literature indicates that ML can have near matched-filter sensitivity under restricted conditions and can provide substantial gains in inference speed, the performance has been found to degrade, as one moves away from Gaussian simulations to real detector noise. Astrophysical claims are not being made based on accuracy or receiver-operating-characteristic scores alone, as such analyses are needed to estimate false-alarm rates for the GW search, to make sure that the results are network coincidental, robust against changes in GW detector state, and significant in the context of the analysis. The paper proposes the use of hybrid systems in which the generation of triggers, the characterization of noise, building vetoes or ranking candidates are accelerated by ML, and the significance is quantified by well-known statistical methods. A realistic noise, a blinded temporal split, a waveform-domain shift test, a time-shift background, a protocol of uncertainty calibration, and a reproducible model reporting scheme, are recommended as a benchmark protocol. Next steps are to make advancements on domain adaptation, self-supervised learning, physics-informed architectures, multimodal detector data, interpretable anomaly searches, and standardized community challenges for third generation and space based detectors.

W7222813948.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant breakthroughs in natural language processing, enabling advanced capabilities in text generation, reasoning, and conversational intelligence. However, a critical limitation persists in the form of hallucinations, where models generate factually incorrect or unverifiable information while maintaining high linguistic confidence. This issue poses substantial risks in high-stakes applications such as healthcare decision support, legal advisory systems, and educational platforms, where accuracy and reliability are paramount. Existing approaches primarily focus on model scaling or fine-tuning, yet they often lack robust mechanisms for real-time verification and interpretability. Addressing this challenge requires a systematic framework capable of detecting, quantifying, and mitigating hallucinated outputs while preserving response fluency and contextual relevance. This paper proposes a hybrid hallucination detection and mitigation framework that integrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), semantic similarity analysis, and a multi-factor confidence scoring mechanism. The system leverages external knowledge sources through vector-based retrieval to validate generated responses and employs transformer-based embeddings to measure semantic consistency between model outputs and verified evidence. A classification layer identifies hallucinated content, followed by a mitigation module that refines responses using grounded contextual information. Experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets such as TruthfulQA and FEVER demonstrates a substantial reduction in hallucination rates and a marked improvement in factual accuracy compared to baseline LLMs. The proposed approach enhances the trustworthiness, explainability, and practical applicability of AI systems, providing a scalable solution for deploying reliable language models in real-world environments.

W7222974994.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in critical domains, where their susceptibility to hallucinations makes reliable and interpretable uncertainty quantification essential. We introduce the concept of mechanistic uncertainty, which characterizes uncertainty through the stability of the internal mechanisms supporting a model's response. We propose the causal robustness margin, defined as the minimum internal intervention required to deviate the model's output, and operationalize it using Jacobian Lens (Jlens) concept steering vectors. Across three open-source models and five question-answering datasets, we show incorrect and uncertain responses exhibit smaller margins, indicating greater sensitivity to internal interventions, and the causal robustness margin complements conventional output-based uncertainty methods. Finally, in a controlled knowledge injection experiment, correctly learned facts show increased margins after training, suggesting that causal robustness provides a mechanistically grounded signal of uncertainty.

W7222977806.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is still the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults. It has a declining median survival rate and shows strong resistance to treatment. This resistance comes from significant differences within the tumor itself. The past failures of standard treatments have led to a shift in neuro-oncology. We now focus on molecular stratification based on genetic changes that can be targeted, instead of relying solely on histopathological classifications. This review looks at how important molecular drivers, like metabolic changes caused by IDH1/2 mutations, MGMT promoter methylation status, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling involving EGFR and EGFRvIII, and changes in epigenetics seen in H3 K27M, are creating new opportunities in immunotherapy, CAR-T cell therapy, precision radiation, and nanomedicine. We also discuss how preclinical validation through in vivo functional models, including patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) and syngeneic mouse lines, offers key insights into tumor evolution under treatment pressure, how drugs penetrate the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and the immunosuppressive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME). However, despite the scientific backing for these therapies, recent Phase III clinical trial failures highlight a significant gap in translating these findings into effective treatments. This gap mainly results from random Darwinian clonal replacement and antigen escape. To address this issue, we explore the potential of liquid biopsies, such as cerebrospinal fluid and plasma, for real-time molecular tracking. These can help differentiate between true progression and pseudoprogression. Ultimately, we believe that closing the translational gap requires moving away from static clinical methods and adopting flexible, long-term trial designs. We also need to integrate multi-omic data with artificial intelligence (AI) to predict cellular changes and counteract resistance mechanisms before they lead to clinical recurrence.

W7223059374.abstract: Answering natural language questions over knowledge graph data is challenging due to the vast number of facts, which can be difficult to process and navigate. One potential solution for this issue is to use mined subgraphs related to the query, although this process still requires extracting these subgraphs. This research presents a solution for extracting subgraphs related to entity candidates from a question-and-answer set, which can be obtained by inferring a large language model by calculating the shortest paths between entities. The proposed approaches detail various features that can be extracted from the subgraphs and reranking models to select the most probable answers from a list of candidates. Experiments were conducted on Wikidata to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. This involved enumerating all the main feature types that can be extracted from mined subgraphs and a detailed analysis of the proposed features and reranking method combinations. In addition, a public web application that provides a useful web tool for studying the graph space between question and answer entities has been developed to work with subgraphs. This includes visualization of the extracted subgraph and automatic generation of natural language text to describe it.

W7223110514.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence and agentic systems can redistribute reading, research, synthesis, criticism, drafting, and coordination within courts. This article asks how that redistribution changes judicial cognition and which institutional safeguards are needed to preserve legitimate adjudication. Through an interdisciplinary narrative review and doctrinal analysis, it develops a framework of institutional intelligence anchored in Brazilian National Council of Justice Resolution No. 615/2025, as amended by Resolution No. 674/2026. Five categories organize the argument: institutional cognitive space describes the allocation of cognitive work; artificial adversariality identifies structured internal challenge among agents; the institutional rein integrates controls over delegated autonomy; meaningful human initiative emphasizes the continuing human authority to frame problems and determine purposes; and institutional AI curation describes the competence required to select, validate, contextualize, and reject artificial contributions. Recent research on human–AI collaboration and multi-agent failure qualifies the framework: neither human review nor artificial disagreement guarantees reliability, and short-term performance gains do not establish long-term professional competence. The article distinguishes technical auditability from legal reason-giving and internal agent debate from the parties’ right to be heard. It proposes workflow-level evaluation and an illustrative protocol connecting permissions, source verification, escalation, and responsibility. Its contribution is a judicial governance synthesis, not an empirically validated architecture. Legitimate delegation depends on preserving institutional competence and contestability throughout the production of decisions, rather than relying exclusively on human approval of a final text.

W7223464978.abstract: By keeping the data separate, federated learning (FL) enables multiple data owners, such as hospitals, edge devices, or financial institutions, to jointly develop a shared machine-learning model, which is of particular relevance in applications of distributed systems that have to be operated under privacy regulation and underlying narrow bandwidth restrictions. We implement both two basic FL mechanisms (Federated Averaging, FedAvg, and a mechanism at the client-side that applies differential-privacy, DP) from the ground-up in NumPy, and test both in a uniform experimental protocol on two different distributed-systems scenarios: a network of 10 simulated healthcare data-silos with the real Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer benchmark (n = 569) and a network of 30 simulated edge/IoT devices with the real UCI handwritten-digits benchmark (n = 1,797). Client data was partitioned both in the near-IID and Dirichlet-skewed NON-IID (Hsu, Qi, & Brown, 2019) regime. In both communication rounds (40 in healthcare and 30 in edge/IoT), federated training achieved 97.7% and 96.7% test accuracy, respectively, (plus or minus 0.6 and 0.4 percentage points, respectively, compared to an equivalent centralized model trained on a “pooled” dataset), but the edge/IoT task suffered significant, monotonic loss of accuracy as the degree of client heterogeneity increased (96.7% for near-IID to 95.4% for the most skewed partition, whereas there was nearly no loss in the healthcare task for which the client models were simpler and near-linearly-separable). The systematic sweep over the differential-privacy noise multiplier confirmed that there is a significantly higher privacy-utility tradeoff for the harder high dimensional edge/IoT task than for the healthcare task (privacy-accuracy tradeoff varied from 96.3% accuracy to 51.1% accuracy as noise varied in the former and 97.7% accuracy to 78.4% accuracy as noise varied in the latter), hence the "cost of privacy" is not an intrinsic property of a differential privacy mechanism but is rather dependent on task difficulty and dimensionality. These results are placed in the context of the federated learning literature in a PRISMA-compliant review of 29 studies. Finally, we present practical suggestions for provisioning communication rounds, client participation percentages, and privacy budgets when rolling out FL across a set of distributed systems with different types and privacy restrictions

W7223693142.abstract: AI-for-Science agents are increasingly being used for formulating scientific hypotheses, running autonomous experiments, and interpreting evidence. These agents are constructed by integrating a large language model (LLM) into a domain-specific agent harness, which in turn can improve the LLM's scientific capability and enable the model to orchestrate scientific tools. In this work, we ask whether model safety is preserved when an LLM is integrated in an AI-for-Science agent harness. We evaluate five agent harnesses on 50 harmful chemistry requests. Specifically, we study how the safety behavior changes under direct prompting, two simple adversarial prompting strategies, and an adaptive attack. Across four recent GPT variants, our results show that the agent harness can increase harmful compliance even under direct prompting. More critically, we find that adaptive attacks that are largely unsuccessful against the base LLM suddenly become highly successful after the agent harness is introduced. Our results show that the safety behavior of the base LLM is not durable once a harness is introduced. Thus, as AI-for-Science agents become more capable and autonomous, the community needs to evaluate and align the agent using domain-specific safety benchmarks.

W7223907446.abstract: Tool-using language model agents are usually evaluated by whether they finish the user's task. That metric misses a common failure: an agent can complete the requested work while also taking an unauthorized side-effecting action, such as writing to the wrong object, expanding the scope of the request, or contacting an unintended recipient. We call this failure mode collateral damage (CD). We introduce SABench (Side-effect-Aware Benchmark), a benchmark of 201 email, calendar, and ticket tasks. Each task crosses one of four state structures (independent, dependent, externally reachable, cross-tool) with one of four trap families (ambiguity, mis-targeting, cascade harm, overreach), and each task has a deterministic trace-based oracle for both goal satisfaction and authorization compliance. Across 2,211 model-task pairs from 11 frontier LLMs spanning major commercial and open model families, 15.2% of all runs incur CD, with risk concentrated in ambiguity tasks (38.8% violation rate) while non-ambiguous traps average 8.4% CD. Among goal-satisfied runs, 12.8% still produce unauthorized writes. Cross-tool and dependent states have about twice the CD rate of independent states. CD rates vary by 4.7x across models at comparable goal rates, which suggests that task success alone is a poor proxy for safe tool use. The SABench task corpus is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Phaedrus/sabench; the traces, oracle, code, and analysis pipeline are released at https://github.com/hjj194/sabench-artifact.

W7223916604.abstract: Sparse outcome rewards make it difficult for long-horizon language-model agents to assign credit to earlier actions. Learned critics provide value estimates for intermediate states, but these estimates can be inaccurate, while estimating intermediate values with repetitive continuation samples from points within a trajectory incurs substantial costs. To mitigate these issues, we introduce FOCUS, an RL method that uses selective branching to help the critic network learn its value estimator. The rollout controller facilitates active learning for the critic by sampling continuations from states that are expected to most reduce the critic's estimation error. These refined value estimates then score the segment between consecutive states with a TD($λ$) advantage, while the sampled evidence supplies training targets for the critic. FOCUS supports long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning through a modular context-management interface that decouples context management from rollout allocation. Our experiments show that using compaction-induced segment boundaries for value estimation and credit assignment, FOCUS outperforms GRPO and VinePPO with matched per-step generation budgets on legal reasoning, deep search, and code localization benchmarks, improving held-out accuracy at Qwen3.5-9B scale by 7.2 points over the strongest baseline on BrowseComp-Plus (55.4 vs. 48.2) and by 4.1 points on DeonticBench (56.5 vs. 52.4).

W7223923051.abstract: Language-model agents combine reasoning, tools, memory, delegation, and external effects. Authority is often distributed across prompts, host code, configuration, and logs. Probabilistic Agentic Programming (PAP) makes responsibility boundaries explicit programming abstractions connecting mandate, authority, effects, and evidence. We compare PAP with programming paradigms, agent-oriented and BDI systems, workflow and policy languages, and LLM tool-use frameworks along seven dimensions. A mediation kernel formalizes checks before tool execution, operation-bound approval, resource limits, and evidence. Inductive proofs establish conditional safety for arbitrary model responses, assuming correct guards and complete mediation. A backward simulation matches graph executions to source executions in a defined sequential Touba subset. Its human checkpoints release program continuations; operation-bound approval remains a separate kernel contract. Finite-state exploration checks the model. Scripted enforcement tests exercise selected refusal paths and permitted controls. An exploratory study combines seven business cases, including two three-agent workflows, seven models from three providers, five methods, and five repetitions per case and method. Shared English instructions and exact checks of stored outcomes yield 1,225 assessed observations. Native Touba completes all 35 observations on six models and 30 on the remaining model; structured Touba ranges from 21 to 35. Native matches the highest observed count for each model, including ties with the frameworks. All paired case intervals include zero. These observed counts describe the evaluated tasks; the runtime authority boundary remains fixed. The results connect responsibility contracts, execution rules, and evidence.

W7223980097.abstract: Materials research relies on scattered and growing data, knowledge, and simulation tools, and a single study often spans multi-day workflows across literature analysis, computation, and experiment. Large language model agents can now retrieve materials data, operate simulation codes, and close design-synthesis-characterization loops with autonomous laboratories. However, extending these agents with new capabilities, keeping long-running tasks on track, and letting them learn from past tasks and user feedback remain difficult. Here we present MatOS, an agent operating system for materials research with three core components: (1) a layered scientific asset graph that organizes data, knowledge, tools, skills, roles, and workflows as reusable assets; (2) a stateful adaptive workflow that runs tasks as explicit execution graphs with scientific checks, so that they can be resumed and traced; and (3) evidence-driven asset evolution, which revises these assets from execution records and user feedback. On ResearchClawBench, MatOS improves on the previously best-performing agent by 11.15% with the same base model and extends the cost-score Pareto frontier. With a common base model, it outperforms Codex CLI and Claude Code, exceeding Codex CLI by 2.13% on MatTools and 4.17% on SciAgentGym. In eight research cases, MatOS narrowed more than 30 million candidate structures to 97 solid-electrolyte candidates, identified 89 halide variants with higher computed conductivity than their parent structures, linked the force errors of 11 pretrained interatomic potentials to local atomic environments, and supported two new methods that reduce errors by 3.1% and 13.6% relative to their baselines. These results show that organizing research capabilities as reusable, evolving assets enables agents to carry out long, multistage materials studies. Code is available at https://github.com/DingyangLyu/MatOS.

W7223995368.abstract: Repeating Transformer layers can improve language-model performance without adding parameters. A pretrained model can be adapted to support both single-pass and looped inference by reusing middle-layer weights for additional computation. Because both paths share weights, training to improve looped predictions can degrade single-pass quality. We study joint training strategies using weighted losses on both outputs, with guidance from the frozen original model. Joint supervision substantially reduces single-pass degradation compared to looped-only training, while preserving looped gains over ordinary continued training. Most of this benefit comes from adjusting the single-pass loss weight, with guidance from the frozen original model further improving the looped output. With validation-selected weights, our method preserves single-pass quality within a predefined tolerance of ordinary continued training while improving looped predictions.

W7224231693.abstract: Multi-agent embodied intelligence systems increasingly integrate vision, language, and sensor-based perception to support collaborative navigation, manipulation, and autonomous decision-making in dynamic environments, but frequent inter-agent communication, redundant large-model inference, and multimodal adversarial attacks can simultaneously increase computational overhead and compromise physical task safety. To address these challenges, this study proposes SafeComm-Agent, a security-aware communication and inference optimization framework that jointly coordinates multimodal attack detection, agent communication, and adaptive reasoning computation. The framework first combines Vision Transformers (ViTs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), cross-modal consistency analysis, and uncertainty estimation to identify anomalous observations and derive agent-level security risks. It then employs a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to construct a dynamic security-aware communication graph, while Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) determines when to communicate, which agents to contact, and what information to transmit; risk-aware message compression and adaptive Test-Time Compute (TTC) further regulate communication and inference budgets, with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) providing additional verification for high-risk states. Experiments in Habitat-based simulated embodied environments with controlled multimodal adversarial perturbations show that SafeComm-Agent achieves a task success rate of 94.6% and an attack detection F1-score of 93.2%. Compared with full-communication MARL, it reduces inference cost by 26%, while achieving a 39% reduction in total computational cost compared with full-communication and full-computation execution. These results demonstrate effective joint optimization of security, communication, and adaptive inference.

W7224639554.abstract: Narrative NLP encompasses a diverse set of competencies such as detecting whether a text contains a narrative, classifying its genre or function, completing its plot, and judging similarity between stories.However, the relationship between model capabilities across these sub-tasks remains poorly understood and no unified benchmark exists to evaluate large language models across these dimensions simultaneously.In this paper, we introduce NARRATOR, a unified benchmark of 96, 818 multiple-choice questions derived from six narrative datasets spanning detection, classification, story completion, and similarity.Evaluating 50 openweight LLMs in a zero-shot setting reveals that LLM performance profiles are highly heterogeneous and no model dominates across all sub-tasks.To exploit this complementarity efficiently, we learn compact narrative competence embeddings of LLMs using a matrix factorisation over a binary correctness matrix, without accessing model weights.A single linear layer on top of these frozen embeddings supports model routing (71.1%), correctness forecasting (65.3%), and benchmark accuracy prediction (mean Kendall's τ = 0.72) at near-zero inference cost.

W7224757321.abstract: Abstract Learning-based intrusion detection produces verdicts operators must simply trust: the audit record is mutable and no independent party endorses the decision. We present BAg-IDS, a distributed detection architecture in which autonomous agents detect, independently re-check, and co-sign every remediation-triggering verdict on a Hyperledger Fabric ledger before it is acted upon, placing certification on the decision path rather than in an after-the-fact log. A calibrated, reliability-weighted ensemble with a reject option feeds the quorum; language-model and governed human-in-the-loop tiers handle escalation. The full stack is implemented and every number measured. Selective certification raises accuracy from 96.6% to 99.7% (0.04% false-positive rate) at 87.3% coverage on CICIDS2017, and reaches 99.98% on the independent GeNIS 2025 corpus while deferring 0.14% of flows. A 360-alert benchmark shows the ~ 2 s consensus latency is structural: one write per key per block forces K votes across at least K blocks, a bound no submission strategy removes.

W7224800887.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is profoundly transforming collaboration across diverse domains by enhancing creativity, decision-making, and human-AI co-creation. This review synthesizes current research on GAI’s integration within knowledge management, environmental monitoring, healthcare, education, and business sectors. It examines key ethical, technical, and psychological challenges, including transparency, alignment, bias, privacy, and workforce disruption. Large Language Models (LLMs), central to GAI advancements, have revolutionized natural language processing but raise concerns around interpretability, trust, and societal impact. This review explores explainability methods, human-aligned training, and fine-tuning strategies that improve reliability and user acceptance. The emergence of LLM-based autonomous agents and multi-agent collaborative frameworks signifies a critical leap toward adaptable, goal-driven AI systems approaching Artificial General Intelligence, highlighting scalability and ethical governance challenges. In healthcare, GAI applications such as ChatGPT and Med-PaLM enhance diagnostics, education, and clinical support, yet demand rigorous ethical oversight and regulatory frameworks to safeguard trust and patient safety. Explainable AI (XAI) further bridges the gap between model complexity and clinical transparency, promoting accountable AI adoption. This review advocates for human-centered, interdisciplinary approaches and scalable, responsible frameworks that balance innovation with ethical stewardship. Future research directions emphasize developing transparent, inclusive, and privacy-preserving GAI systems that maximize societal benefits while mitigating risks across sectors.

W7224912465.abstract: Despite considerable breakthroughs in renoprotective medicines, chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remain the predominant causes of end-stage renal disease and cardiovascular morbidity. Growing evidence shows that oxidative stress is not simply a result of renal injury but a crucial pathogenic element interconnecting metabolic dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and fibrogenesis. Physiological ROS mediate cellular signaling, mitochondrial homeostasis, and adaptive responses. Persistent redox imbalance, by contrast, results in excessive production of ROS by dysfunctional mitochondria, NADPH oxidases, uremic toxins, and hyperglycemia-driven metabolic pathways that drive self-amplifying oxidative circuits that accelerate nephron loss. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the existing knowledge on the molecular causes of oxidative stress in CKD and DKD, with a focus on disease-specific pathways such as mitochondrial dysfunction, AGE–RAGE signaling, metabolic memory, insulin resistance, and lipotoxicity. It also describes cell-specific oxidative injury in podocytes, mesangial cells, tubular epithelial cells, and endothelial cells, and how these contribute to glomerular dysfunction, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and disease progression. Emerging redox-targeted strategies, such as mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, NADPH oxidase inhibitors, Nrf2 activators, and sirtuin modulation, are reviewed in terms of experimental rationale and clinical evidence. We discuss established renoprotective therapies, such as RAAS inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, and GLP-1 receptor agonists, separately to distinguish demonstrated clinical benefits from the still incompletely established contribution of redox mechanisms. The clinical use of circulating and urinary oxidative stress biomarkers is also critically evaluated. Finally, we discuss new research directions in precision redox medicine, including cell-specific antioxidant delivery, redox-sensitive molecular imaging, integration of multi-omics, artificial intelligence-assisted biomarker discovery, and human-relevant translational models, as well as the current stages of development and barriers to clinical application. The present review combines mechanistic evidence with biomarker and translational studies to prioritize research in biomarker-informed risk stratification and mechanism-guided redox therapies in CKD and DKD. However, their clinical utility remains to be proven and requires independent validation and prospective evidence of improved patient outcomes. These advances provide a foundation for biomarker-informed risk stratification and mechanism-guided therapy in CKD and DKD, but clinical use requires further validation and evidence of improved patient outcomes.

W7225078571.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming Smart Healthcare Systems (SHS) from conventional data-driven infrastructures into intelligent ecosystems capable of autonomous perception, reasoning, collaboration, adaptation, and clinical decision support. The emergence of Agentic AI represents a significant transition toward autonomous healthcare intelligence, in which AI agents can dynamically perceive clinical contexts, plan and execute tasks, interact with heterogeneous medical resources, collaborate with other agents, and continuously adapt to changing healthcare conditions. Despite this potential, the adoption of Agentic AI in healthcare remains constrained by critical concerns involving patient privacy, cyber security, explainability, reliability, accountability, trust, and safe continual learning. This survey reviews recent advances in trustworthy Agentic AI for healthcare, focusing on Federated Learning, Zero Trust Security, Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning, and Privacy-Preserving Intelligence. It analyzes how these technologies support secure collaboration, protect sensitive medical data, enhance interpretability, and enable continuous learning in distributed healthcare environments. The paper also highlights key limitations in existing approaches, particularly the absence of unified frameworks that jointly address autonomy, security, privacy, and trust. Finally, it outlines open research challenges and future directions toward building reliable and explainable Agentic AI systems for Smart Healthcare.

W7225125257.abstract: The rapid growth of agentic systems has created a pressing need for rigorous and reproducible methods to quantify their degree of autonomy. Existing approaches rely on behavioral logs, task completion rates, or subjective expert judgment, all of which are resource intensive and difficult to generalize across deployment contexts. This work introduces a diagram driven framework that measures agentic system autonomy through structural and semantic analysis of diagrams that capture agent activities and data flow between agents, such as process, workflow, or interaction diagrams. We extract a fourteen dimensional visual feature vector encoding arrow directionality, arrowhead density, actor and activity distribution, edge structure, and image entropy and combine it with high dimensional feature representations from using two datasets. To assess model robustness and generalizability, we conducted a comparative experiment with ten existing works. Our evaluation shows that the proposed model consistently outperforms the baseline backbones under both experimental settings, providing a strong foundation for scalable assessment of autonomous agentic systems. These findings suggest that our approach can serve as a flexible blueprint for evaluating a broad class of autonomous agentic systems across diverse tasks and environments.

W7225145035.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are rapidly evolving with different use cases being undertaken across critical domains, such as finance, cybersecurity, and autonomous operations. These systems introduce new and complex attack vectors that go beyond those found in traditional computing systems or conventional machine learning models. This includes challenges arising from autonomous decision-making, inter-agent communication, and environmental interactions. As Agentic AI systems gain prominence, new threats are uncovered, exposing a fast-expanding surface for attacks. In the case of multi-agent systems, their distributed nature, which is also a key advantage in providing scalability and adaptability, amplifies the potential for adversarial exploitation. Despite the increasing awareness that new attack vectors are still being discovered, the landscape of threats specific to Agentic AI remains fragmented, without a comprehensive resource available to guide researchers. This paper addresses that gap by reviewing the current state of knowledge regarding known threats to Agentic AI.

W7225147389.abstract: Standard attention forms query (Q), key (K), and value (V) matrices through learned linear projections of input hidden states. Architectures such as GAU and Mega incorporate nonlinear transformations into attention. In this paper, we propose GatedV, a simple attention variant that applies SiLU only to V before aggregation without introducing additional trainable parameters. We evaluate GatedV against a standard decoder-only Transformer using matched parameter counts, paired initializations, and equal training-token budgets. At 2.33M parameters, GatedV reduces mean held-out perplexity from 59.1 to 57.9 (2.0%), with improvements across all five paired seeds. At 26.16M parameters, following an equal-budget learning-rate search, mean held-out perplexity falls from 20.2 to 19.7 (2.4%), with improvements across all three paired seeds. Small-model ablations show that the tested affine rescaling of values does not fully reproduce GatedV's gains. A short interleaved benchmark on NVIDIA DGX Spark measures approximately 0.7% higher full-context forward latency for the larger model, based on synchronized wall-clock timings. These findings suggest that value-only self-gating can improve language modeling performance without increasing parameter count or redesigning the attention-weighting mechanism.

W7225326491.abstract: Web applications change so often that manual testing cannot keep up, and scripted automation breaks whenever the user interface changes. Large language models (LLMs) and the agent systems built on them offer a different approach: software agents that observe an application, decide what to do, act through a browser, and judge the result. This paper reviews how such agents are applied to web application testing. We organize existing work around five stages of the testing lifecycle (requirement analysis, test generation, execution, oracle and defect detection, and reporting), compare single-agent and multi-agent architectures, and examine how agentic testers are evaluated. We collect the challenges that keep recurring: hallucination, non-determinism, cost, weak evaluation practice, and safety. The reviewed work automates isolated stages, and a system that handles the whole lifecycle with little manual scripting has not yet been demonstrated. We therefore propose a five-agent workflow, built on LangGraph, Playwright, a locally hosted open-source model, and PostgreSQL, for end-to-end autonomous testing, and we outline a protocol for evaluating it. The paper presents a design and a literature-based analysis only; it reports no experimental results of its own.

W7225396619.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced multilingual NLP significantly, yet their effectiveness for Bengali, a globally important but low-resource language, remains understudied due to limited linguistic resources and the absence of a standardized evaluation benchmark. This is due to the unavailability of large linguistic resources and the lack of a standard benchmarking framework, which has yet to be established. This study aims to address the underrepresentation of Bengali text classification by leading a systematic evaluation. It involves assessing multiple open-weight LLMs on Bengali text classification tasks and observing their limitations and regular error patterns. The procedure consists of six open-weight LLMs, which include LLaMA-3.2-3B, Mistral-V3-7B, DeepSeek-R1-8B, Phi-4-14B, Gemma-2-27B, and Qwen-2.5-72B, and are evaluated using four critical text classification tasks in Bengali, namely sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, hate-speech detection, and fake-news classification. Furthermore, two prompting methods are compared in the context of zero-shot and few-shot prompting using both the vLLM inference engine and Hugging Face Transformers pipelines to investigate the adaptability of the models in resource-limited settings. Across all four tasks, the two largest models (Qwen-2.5-72B and Gemma-2-27B) obtained the highest scores, although the ranking was not strictly monotonic in parameter count and, because each scale is represented by a single model family, the design cannot attribute these differences to model size alone. When training in zero-shot, Qwen-2.5-72B showed the best performance at 79.90% accuracy and 79.88% Macro-F1 score, showing amazing accuracy on hate-speech detection. In the case of fake news, Gemma-2-27B performed best at 84.45% accuracy and 84.33% Macro-F1 score. With a few-shot set-up, Gemma-2-27B and Qwen-2.5-72B demonstrated a high level of performance in terms of Macro-F1 score, reaching 84.17% for fake-news detection and 66.80% for emotion recognition, respectively. Paired multi-model tests (Cochran's Q with Holm-corrected McNemar post-hoc comparisons) confirmed significant differences among the six models across all tasks and prompting settings, whereas the effect of five-shot prompting, obtained with a single fixed demonstration set, was significant for only 4 of 24 model-task combinations after correction and never for the three largest models. The findings characterise benchmark classification performance under the evaluated settings rather than real-world effectiveness, and indicate that model scale, multilingual pre-training, and in-context demonstrations are jointly associated with, but cannot be causally isolated as drivers of, performance on Bengali text classification.

W7225456810.abstract: In distributed and heterogeneous computing environments, federated machine learning has proven to be a viable approach to privacy-preserving predictive analytics. This study introduced a federated system for anomaly detection to aid in collaborative learning and distributed decision intelligence, without aggregating raw network data on the central server. An unsupervised federated autoencoder was applied to learn traffic representations across decentralized clients, and Federated Averaging was applied to collect locally trained model parameters into a global model. To assess the model performance, reconstruction loss, accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and ROC AUC were calculated. The federated model shows that the mean reconstruction loss gradually decreases with the number of communication rounds, indicating convergence, and the loss in the 10th communication round is 0.6754, which is approximately a 32.14% decrease from the loss in the 1st communication round. With respect to recognition of benign traffic, the model attained accuracy rate of 70.44% and specificity of 91.96% which is good. The attack recall was however, limited to 6.36%, F1-score of 9.76% and ROC-AUC of 0.365, which showed that the system discriminated poorly between malicious and non-malicious observations. The results indicate that convergence from a federated perspective does not always result in intrusion detection success. The study also highlights the importance of adaptive aggregation.
